I'm so glad that you're going to spend your morning with us. We are here for another episode of Alternatives Access, and I think it's going to be a really special episode. I have a friend and favorite colleague from H. I, g capital, Jordan Griffin, who's an executive managing partner and also the co-president of Tam, their Total Access Middle Market strategy. And I'm thrilled to get her to dive into the middle market and why it's going to matter for portfolios as we move into a more complex world. With that, we'll just get started. Jordan, thanks for joining us. I'm so excited to be here. I feel like I'm hanging out with you all the time. I love it. It's going to be a fun time. Jordan and I have actually had a conversation on the middle market a handful of times over the last couple of months, and I think what's been interesting is every single time we chat, I learned something new. Oh, good. And well, and I think that's because the middle market, there's so much there that I think gets taken for granted, almost. With that, I think we should just start with why the middle market is compelling and and really how you would define it. So if we jump to idea one, maybe we just spend a moment on this segment in this part of the market, the why why in particular that you've spent a number of years investing in this space? Let me first define it because everyone defines middle market differently for today's conversation. Think of total enterprise value of less than 1 billion. And you're absolutely right. Why now for middle market I think I'm stealing a line from you that you once said to me. It's really why always it really needs to be a core part of anyone's private equity portfolio. But let me simplify the middle market opportunity in three things one, it's scale, it's inefficiency, and it's white space for operational improvement. First and foremost, the middle market is a large and deep market and it's highly fragmented. There are over 535,000 companies globally that are total value of less than 1,000,200,000 just here in the US. Now that big of market sourcing is key and we can talk a bit about that today. But that is key. But in addition you just have a plethora of great businesses, market leaders, strong cash flowing businesses. But many, and I'm generalizing here a bit tend to be under managed. Now that presents two great opportunities. One, you can buy them cheaper, but to be paths and optionality for value creation is much wider with an under managed business. I also really like the cellar dynamics in the middle market. It's partnership focus versus valuation focus. So 70% of global GDP is driven by family owned businesses. And when they are thinking about selling certainly maximizing price is up there. But they're also thinking about their legacy. They're thinking about their culture fit. So that allows more of a relationship partnership aspect as a buyer. Sure. And then when you're dealing with a market this large and deep, of course it's going to be less efficient. It's going to be less transparent. I love that that leads to less competition. You're not going to see as many of these robust auction processes where everybody and their brother is bidding and they're bidding up, up, up into valuation, that's pretty untenable. That happens less frequently. 97% of off market opportunities are found within the middle market. So as you can see, there's a lot to love in terms of structural inefficiencies, but also opportunities that the middle market provides. Sure. I mean, a lot to love, but even more so just a lot to do. I think so many of our clients are now thinking about investing in private equity as a potential part of their portfolio for outsized returns or diversification, so on and so forth. But I think what's increasingly compelling here is this is what I would argue is maybe one of the truest forms of active management because of the ability to value, create, to partner alongside founders and families who may be looking to sell. So really interesting part of the market. What I want to make sure we sort of define in today's conversation is really that this is a subset of private equity. And so when our clients are maybe thinking about investing in the space more broadly in private markets, this is just one way to access private companies. There are plethora of other places that clients can continue to invest, but we'll spend some time diving in here. The next idea that I think is compelling, and you alluded to this, but it's really so many factors. But the reason why you invest in private equity is for the potential for outsized returns. Take us through what historical performance in this asset class has looked like. While we won't guarantee or promise what future returns will look like, I do think that history can be informative of sort of what you're looking at. And so maybe take us through how you're thinking about long term potential for outperformance, but also what historically the middle market has done. Yeah, absolutely. There has been tremendous outperformance in private equity as well as in the middle market. You know, I think all of us who are active investors in private equity, we really seek it out in our portfolio as a core allocation. But it's because it's able to deliver uncorrelated alpha relative to public equities. However, I don't know that everyone is focused on the middle market when they think private equity, and they absolutely should be. If you look at today's private equity market, 87% of deal volume based on deal count is in the middle market 87%. So if you're making an allocation to private equity and you're trying to drive for that alpha generation and you're only focus on large cap and mega cap, you're only seeing 13% of the market. And that comes into play not only on acquisition, but we'll talk a bit about exit. You know, in order to be successful and to drive that outperformance. To me it's sourcing. Well it's buying right. It's driving value creation and then having strong exit execution. But as you're looking at those four components, putting them all together is what's going to lead to this outperformance. If you see this chart here and we dissect the returns a bit going back to 2007, middle market private equity has delivered two and a half times greater growth than the S&P 500. But if we dissect that even further, it's not only outperforming public equities, but it's also outperforming mega cap growth equity buyout in general. And part of that is because it's such a large swath of the private equity universe. So I'm not saying you need to pick one or the other. I think it's really important that you do have a diversified portfolio within your private equity allocation. Well, and I think, too, in the spirit of diversification, I also think there is this layer of and I think sort of the natural next question is there's more opportunity here. You have the potential for outperformance, but is there also the potential for greater risk. So maybe just spend a quick moment on what the risk look like in this part of the market relative to maybe large cap, which most people are typically more familiar with? Right. Thinking about the idea that maybe a larger business is more insulated from some of the maybe the macro things that take place or management issues and so on and so forth. Yeah, absolutely. I think one way to look at risk in general is where are you buying a company? Sure. And so a lot of that comes down to your entry multiple. And within the middle market, we've been able to achieve a lot lower attachment points on the onset. So we're all familiar. In 2021 there is a huge value trap. People were overpaying and over leveraging for businesses. That is absolutely what you should try to avoid because it can occur during various market cycles. But if I go back to 2021 and I look at the entry multiples over the last five years, large cap was buying companies at 15.5 times entry multiple. The middle market is buying companies four times cheaper at 11.6 times. So what does that mean? That's actually a great springboard for downside protection but also asymmetric risk return on the downside protection area. If you are buying a company at eight, nine, ten times entry multiple, and you're getting your leverage for that company from private debt investors who are focused on downside protection themselves, they're not going to lend to you at high loan to value ratios. In fact, it's going to be moderate to low loan to value ratio. They're looking to protect themselves. And so we appreciate it's a smaller company. There's going to be lower leverage. So right there you're kind of avoiding the second part of that equation of over leveraging. But you're also less likely to overpay. And that four times cheaper valuation. It provides a bit of a valuation cushion. And it also helps absorb earnings shocks. But taking a step back it's not just about where you're buying it. You will tend to see middle market portfolios to be much more diversified in terms of the number of portfolio companies. So not anyone deal is going to make or break a fund, and not anyone deal is going to lose an entire fund. So I think that's a big mitigate. The opportunity set though is robust. You have significant pass in terms of the value creation playbook that you can apply to a company that you've bought at a ten times entry multiple, and that operational framework, which is going to lead to ultimately creating a very attractive value creation story. Increases also your paths on exits. And the best way to de-risk a portfolio is to exit a company. Well and I think to and you you talked us through idea three which is great. And so maybe we flash it for for everyone who wants to take in those data points. I think what's really nice about about this slide is, you know, you sort of make it really clear in entry at lower multiples, less leverage, just inherently really across the sector. But definitely that what you've been focused on is investor. You have all of the potential from a value creation perspective operational improvement but exits. And to really that takes us to our fourth idea. And we're just grooving this morning on this. But I think what's really interesting here is the last three years, every conversation I've had with clients who have invested in large cap private equity, for the most part, have had delayed or slow distributions relative to what they thought would be the case in the middle market. You haven't necessarily seen that, and I think that's because of less reliance on the IPO. Markets take us through the middle market specifically, and even the lower middle market in more particular just around exit opportunity, one with those exits can look like. But then also sort of the strategic levers you all have around exiting to, to different places. Yeah. As I mentioned, one of the best ways to de-risk your portfolio is to solidify your marks, to generate realizations, to distribute capital back to your investors. That's investor favorite part. And hopefully you're doing that at Target Returns or even better above target returns. But you want to be in control of your own destiny on the exit. You know, having just 1 or 2 paths can be very limiting. The beauty of the middle market is we have multiple paths to exit. Certainly, the IPO market is a path. It's not the biggest path. Definitely not a huge component. When you start talking about lower middle market companies. And as much as IPOs are really attractive, they're never exactly a full exit. Sometimes they're more of a capital markets transaction, but you could have the best company and have perfectly executed your value creation plan and you're ready to exit. And if that IPO window is shut and that's really your only path, then you're not able to de-risk your portfolio and you're not able to get distributions back to your clients. You're left hanging out a bit in the middle market, right? That is a path, certainly, but you're also very much selling to strategic buyers. You're selling to financial sponsors, larger private equity firms. And because of where the middle market sits, the number of upper middle market managers, large cap managers, even mega cap managers is enormous. So you have a much wider group of people to be potential buyers. And I think what's nice about what you're describing to we we had some recent conversations with some of our partners, and what they were describing is as it becomes harder or even less attractive to be a publicly traded company today, at least in the US, where it's a much more expensive endeavor than it was 20 years ago. Private equity markets have become incredibly efficient and also quite large. And so to your point, this ability to even sell up market to upper middle market or large cap sponsors is a really material exit opportunity because there are so many, but also because they're so large. The capital does exist in these markets today, which I think is pretty interesting. Absolutely. And if you look at just the statistics alone, the middle market has been incredibly active on exits. It does similar to how it makes up the large majority of deal volume at acquisition. It also makes up the large majority of deal activity.. Exactly 94% of exits that you have seen in private equity have occurred within the middle market based on deal count. That's a staggering number. Well, one of the things that you also alluded to, I guess, on our prior idea was the operational improvement or the value creation abilities. And I think that's what I want to spend the most time on today, because I think sometimes it's taken for granted that, you know, you don't just buy a company, cross your fingers and then look to exit at a greater multiple. And we all win, really. In particular, in the middle market space, there's work to be done. We're rolling up our sleeves. And so take us through idea five. And this is sort of this hands on operational approach. What does a value creation actually look like. Because it's not crossing your fingers and hoping. No it's definitely not. In fact, if you are relying on multiple expansion or financial engineering to be the hallmark of how you're going to drive returns, that will be a failed strategy in today's environment. And this has been a statistic that's been quoted pretty often recently. But in today's environment, if you're trying to hit a 20% IRR and a two and a half times cash on cash return, you have to grow annual EBITDA by 12% year over year. That is a huge shift from ten years ago. Where to achieve the same return, you only were required 5% growth. So what? That tells me, it tells me that the bar has risen, right? It tells me that you have to earn the return via hands on operational approach to value creation. That can take on a lot of different flavors. It can be accelerating revenues, operational efficiencies, or upgrading or building a management team. In the middle market, you see a fair amount of corporate carve outs. You are then lifting up an actual management team to that. But the more important aspect is identifying on day one. Why is it attractive to buy this company? What is it about this company that during our ownership we can effectuate change and drive value creation? And that value creation playbook shouldn't be aspirational. It needs to be highly achievable. Right? So when we're underwriting a business, we don't include multiple expansion and we don't include strategic M&A. Those are a bit outside of our control. We have a very systematic value creation. And each company requires a different approach. But it's identifying that and then also having the hands on expertise to execute it. It may be great that you've identified it, but if you don't have anyone that can deliver on it, that will also be challenging as well. And I think one of the things that has been interesting over time, as we've spent more time in the middle market in particular, is this idea around having a team large enough to your point to actually execute on something like this? Talk a little bit about it. Maybe we just lean for another moment into the risk here. In a world like today, when I think about inflation hovering where it is, interest rates kind of hanging out where they are and have been for the last year. How do these things impact the operational improvements you can bring to a company, even just in this world of AI? I would imagine that smaller companies have a harder time effectuate these things, and so a manager who can step in and bring value creation in this form could be really, really accretive to their already existing businesses because I mean, historically, right, you haven't invested in businesses that aren't already profitable, that are already revenue generating. Right. We're investing in good businesses from start. But what does that look like just being a smaller company. How they adopt change in this way? No, I think you're absolutely right. I mean, with smaller companies in and of itself, sometimes they're not kind of able to institutionalize it and take it to the next level. We love under managed businesses. We like to buy complexity, but we're ultimately trying to sell simplicity. And that's key. But having expertise where it's a repeatable playbook, where we've done it time and time again of identifying a company that has too much customer concentration. But we see a path, and we have operating partners to deliver on how we're going to diversify that customer concentration. That's a very achievable value creation lever that you can pull. I think AI is core to every underwrite that we do. It's core to every private equity managers underwrite that they do and is AI disruptor and something that is very difficult to solve and maybe outside of your control to solve. Or actually, is it a benefit and productivity tool? A smaller company is underutilized in that area, and bringing resources of very established private equity managers that can provide operating partners to institutionalize their AI approach is incredibly beneficial. Again, we talk about risk, and you do think of smaller companies as having greater risk, but in many ways, because you're buying it so much cheaper. You build in a buffer, and there's so much more to do with that business. If something's incredibly a well, well old machine and operating on all cylinders, you're sort of wondering where where am I going to get my 12% annual EBITDA growth? And that's the dynamic that I think is incredibly attractive in our market of it. Well, you've absolutely made the case for middle market. As always. I learned something new from you. I love this idea around entering complexity, selling simplicity. I'm going to steal that for me. But I think more importantly, just another lever for our clients to have in their toolkits or to pull on their own right. Knowing more about the private equity space and what you can do to diversify your portfolios. We're so focused on building in durability, particularly in markets that look like today. So hopefully you all take away some ideas as well. Jordan, I can't thank you enough for your time. It's been a pleasure for all of you who spent your morning with us, I appreciate it. Hopefully it was a great 20 minutes and we will catch you next time for all to access. Thank you for joining us. Morgan Global Research has dropped a sobering message and reversed its "one and done" forecast on Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes. The Wall Street brokerage now calls for two additional increases, plus one in December, to tame persistent price pressures amid higher short-term borrowing costs. This means consumers and businesses can expect the interest rates on credit cards, student loans, and home-equity loans to rise through early 2027, and indirectly, mortgage rates and Treasury bond yields will also be influenced. As for investors, higher interest rates ripple through the stock market and investor portfolios via several core channels ranging from discounted cash flows and corporate borrowing costs to shifts in asset allocation. Back in September, I reported that J.P. Morgan economists called for only one additional 25-basis-point-rate hike by the central bank to curb sticky inflation fueled by the energy shocks from the Iran War and the supply-demand dynamic of artificial intelligence. But in a Nov. 19 client note obtained by Reuters, J.P. Morgan economists call for additional 25 basis-point-rate hikes at the Federal Open Market Committee's January and March meetings. "These ​hikes aren't to deliver a bad labor ​market, but to preserve credibility when they have ⁠no compelling narrative for a pause," J.P. ​Morgan strategists led by Michael Feroli said. This falls in line with what other Fed watchers and even what Fed officials are signaling: inflation is coming in way too hot. It's not only time for higher interest rates, but these hikes may in fact be overdue. "The labor market has not been a ​source of ​inflationary pressure, ⁠and yet inflation remains elevated," J.P. Morgan said, adding it expects modest, positive ​job growth next year. Brokerages BofA Global Research ⁠and Deutsche Bank also expect the central ​bank to increase the benchmark federal funds rate by 25 basis points at each of its next three meetings. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to dispense with forward guidance to markets after taking over the role in May has left the U.S. monetary policy path without an "overarching narrative," J.P. Morgan said. Forward guidance is a communication tool that the Fed used to signal the future path of monetary policy and interest rates to the public and financial markets in order to influence economic behavior and manage expectations. "Without a narrative as a pole star, policy ​is more likely to be reactive to incoming ​data," J.P. Morgan said. As I reported, minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee October meeting released Nov. 18, along with some very pointed public remarks from top Fed officials, show the U.S. central bank is becoming increasingly alarmed that price pressures are moving away from its 2% target, but there's a wide range of opinion within its ranks as to the best approach to lower price pressures. For investors, businesses and consumers, the emerging consensus signals that hopes for interest-rate relief in 2027 have all but evaporated. In fact, when the FOMC held its benchmark short-term interest rate steady at 3.75% to 4% in October with a divisive 10-2 vote, the minutes show several participants described the pause as a "close call." The CME Group's FedWatch Tool  projects roughly a 100% probability of a rate hike at the FOMC December meeting, a 48% probability of another in January 2027. The FedWatch Tool puts the probability of another 25-basis-point raise at the FOMC's March 2027 meeting at approximately 58%, suggesting traders increasingly expect additional monetary tightening early next year. At that point, traders expect the federal funds target range will have reached 4.25% to 4.50%. Related: Fed rate-cut hopes for 2027 take a stunning turn Four Fed Governors — Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Michael Barr, Lisa Cook and Christopher Waller — signaled decidedly hawkish tones in the past week, expressing that further tightening of policy was necessary to bring inflation back to its 2% target — a goal the central bank has missed for nearly six years. Waller doubled down on his comments earlier this month, saying that rising price pressures call for a jumbo 50-basis-point rate hike in December. "You might need to, like, shock people," he said in a Nov. 18 CNBC interview. Warsh has repeatedly said that the Fed is committed to its dual mandate: use interest rates and balance-sheet policy to keep prices stable and the labor market at full employment. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who will be a voting member of the FOMC in 2027, said in a Nov. 19 conference call with reporters that he will consider all options when policymakers meet again Dec. 8-9 to set interest rates. He did not push back against the possibility of a larger-than-usual interest rate increase. "The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy. I find it hard to…look at that any other way," Goolsbee said. "When you're getting major business investment, almost unprecedented levels of business investment, there's a high danger ​that the economy's capacity cannot handle that kind of a pig through the python." President Donald Trump has been criticizing the Fed for nearly a decade for not lowering interest rates to 1% or lower. He repeated his demands during a press conference Nov. 20, saying interest rates are high because the central bank's leaders are "too political." "Whenever we announce good numbers, they raise the rates. They do that for a reason,'' Trump said. "They do that to destroy the country." The growing prospect of another round of interest-rate increases keeps the independent central bank on a collision course with the Trump administration's calls for cheaper borrowing costs. For consumers, businesses and investors, the message from Wall Street is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: The era of waiting for lower interest rates may take longer than anyone wants. title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks - The Guardian
content: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost. In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger. Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters. Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”. JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk. Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported. title: JP Morgan Chase — Cybersecurity Breach Exposed Following Major System Outage - The Korea Daily
content:
Major financial institution JP Morgan Chase suffered a cyberattack through an external vendor just three days after experiencing a massive computer system outage, resulting in the potential leakage of customer information. Alongside Chase, major global card networks Visa and Mastercard also reported exposure of customer data. According to Reuters, JP Morgan Chase stated that an external partner was targeted by a cyberattack, which may have compromised certain customer information. The hackers may have accessed marketing materials containing customer names and email addresses. The hacking group ‘n0n’ claimed on the 16th that it had secured customer information from Chase, Visa, and Mastercard, subsequently releasing related data. The data verified by Reuters contained email addresses of approximately 16,000 Chase customers and 124 employees, along with some phone numbers and postal codes, though the authenticity of the leaked data has not been independently verified. Some of the exposed data is reportedly linked to Chase’s invitation-only credit card program targeting customers with assets exceeding $10 million. Visa and Mastercard also experienced breaches through external vendors. Visa noted that its Asia-Pacific regional partner was targeted, with leaked data including email addresses and phone numbers of customers in South Korea, Japan, Taiwan, and Hong Kong. However, Visa emphasized that its internal network and payment information, such as card numbers, remained unaffected. The record $6.3 billion Binance hack, tied to North Korea, laid bare how aggressively state and criminal actors are targeting financial infrastructure, while a wave of breaches has hit crypto firms through third-party vendors, echoing the vendor weakness at the center of this latest incident. The payments giants have all leaned deeper into crypto and stablecoins this year, from Visa and Mastercard's settlement programs to JPMorgan's growing digital-asset footprint, making their security posture increasingly relevant to the onchain economy they're racing to join. JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Visa (V), and Mastercard (MA) said on Thursday that some select customer data, including names and emails, was accessed by attackers after a cyberattack on a vendor. Spokespeople for the companies said no payments or card data was leaked and that their own systems were not affected by the incident. JPMorgan said it believes hackers who attacked a third-party vendor accessed marketing data, including customer names and email addresses. The bank also said the incident isn't related to outages many of its customers reported earlier this week, which it blamed on a software bug. "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. "We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," a Mastercard spokesperson said. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the person added. A Visa spokesperson added claims of the incident are associated to a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region. "This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week," the Visa spokesperson added. A ransomware group known as n0n has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the dark web and shared sample data as proof, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar. The cybersecurity firm told Yahoo Finance that it hasn't independently verified whether the ransomware group carried out the intrusion. It also supported JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard's statements that the breaches most likely originated at a third-party vendor and involved marketing and benefit-program data such as names and email addresses. "The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," SOCRadar chief information security officer Ensar Seker said in an emailed statement. The latest incident comes as consumers are on high alert after a string of major technology outages this November. title: Visa, Mastercard, and JP Morgan Chase customer data reportedly compromised - WBAL News Radio
content: Data from thousands of Visa, Mastercard and JP Morgan Chase customers was leaked Thursday by a ransomware group, according to several reports. It’s the latest in a string of tech incidents that have unnerved customers across the U.S. over the past two weeks. Though the scope and source of the information remain unclear, The Wall Street Journal reports that thousands of customers’ data was involved. The incident has not disrupted payment services and is not linked to banking problems from earlier this week. JPMorgan Chase said Thursday that attackers targeted third-party service providers and may have accessed marketing data, including some customer names and email addresses. The bank said the incident was not connected to service disruptions customers experienced earlier in the week. JPMorgan Chase did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party providers that were targeted. “Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” a JPMorgan Chase statement said. Visa also confirmed a security incident involving a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. Its own systems were not affected, and there was no indication that payment data, including card numbers, had been compromised, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. A Mastercard spokesperson said hackers accessed a limited amount of information belonging to some cardholders enrolled in a particular benefits program. The spokesperson said Mastercard contained the exposure and that its payment network and customers’ ability to use their cards were unaffected. The news comes after several days of technology outages across the U.S. disrupted air travel, email and hotel bookings, and compromised classified internal communications at the National Security Agency. Third-party platforms that provide services to JPMorgan Chase were hit by a cyberattack that may have exposed some customer data such as names and email addresses, the banking giant said Thursday. The disclosure comes amid a wave of technical outages that have disrupted services across federal networks and private company systems, including a "software bug" found in JPMorgan Chase systems that halted online banking on Monday. In an X post on Thursday, the company said there is "no connection" between the third-party cyberattack and the disruption to its online banking services earlier this week. "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors," the company said in its statement on X, adding that the information accessed "may include customer names and email addresses." Cyberattacks targeting third-party services have become increasingly common in recent years, in part because those platforms often have access to a range of different companies and their respective data. In 2024, health care IT firm Change Healthcare experienced a ransomware attack that compromised the sensitive medical data of more than 100 million people. And last year, a hack of Oracle's E-Business Suite compromised data at Cox Enterprises, The Washington Post and Harvard University. The recent storm of outages has left the banking industry and federal regulators on high alert for more disruptions. At a major banking conference earlier this week, panelists and attendees warned of threats posed by artificial intelligence, particularly as frontier models have become better at finding and exploiting security flaws at an unseen speed and scale. Recently released meeting minutes from the Federal Reserve's October gathering showed that some Fed officials noted that cyberattacks are a "critical area of concern" for financial stability. In September, federal bank regulators proposed new guidance instructing banks to focus third-party provider risk management on "core" financial risks that could affect their balance sheets, deprioritizing nonessential activities. In a statement to POLITICO, JPMorgan Chase emphasized that they are still abiding by the standing interagency guidance, which does not shift that emphasis. "Regardless of any proposal, we have strengthened our controls and risk management of third parties — a focus of ours for some time now," said Patricia Wexler, a spokesperson for JPMorgan Chase. title: Bank Customers Don't Trust AI With Their Money, And Citigroup (NYSE: C), JPMorgan (NYSE: JPM), And Schwab (NYSE: SCHW) Are Counting On It - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 19, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Only 49% of bank customers trust the accuracy of AI-generated financial information, compared with 79% who trust information sourced directly from bank websites, according to recent survey data. That credibility gap is proving to be a significant asset for major financial institutions as they push back against the growing ambitions of third-party AI agents seeking access to customer accounts. The conversation intensified following Meta Platforms’ (NASDAQ: META) September launch of Muse, a personal AI agent that drew widespread media attention and renewed speculation about artificial intelligence upending traditional banking. Concerns about Muse and similar tools center on scenarios where agents autonomously move money across accounts or exploit credit card reward systems at scale, potentially eroding core banking revenue streams. Yet the industry’s response has been less panic and more coordinated resistance, with several of the country’s largest financial institutions drawing clear boundaries around customer account access. Citigroup (NYSE: C), Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), and JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) have each announced they will refuse third-party AI agents or assistants permission to interact with customer accounts. Charles Schwab (NYSE: SCHW) CEO Rick Wurster struck a measured tone on the issue, telling Bloomberg last month that relatively few of the firm’s clients are even attempting to reach their accounts through unauthorized AI agents. A separate survey finding reinforces the banks’ position further, with 72% of customers expressing hesitation about sharing their financial data with generative AI tools at all. Without regulatory clarity defining the rules, liability frameworks, and permissible limits for agentic AI in financial services, banks are expected to maintain and potentially tighten those restrictions. The more telling strategic move, however, is what banks are building behind those walls, with institutions racing to develop proprietary AI products that keep customers engaged within their own ecosystems. Schwab has already unveiled an AI assistant called Charley, while JPMorgan has begun a targeted pilot of a tool named Smart Cash, designed to forecast users’ cash flow and automatically shift funds to maximize yield. By building in-house alternatives, banks are effectively using the competitive pressure from companies like Meta as a catalyst rather than a threat, channeling it into product development that strengthens customer retention. As one analyst put it plainly, “Banks are AI beneficiaries, not AI roadkill,” a framing that captures the industry’s current posture with notable precision. The emerging picture is one of an industry that has chosen to absorb and redirect technological disruption rather than cede ground to outside platforms competing for control of customer financial relationships. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

Morgan Asset Management today announced the launch of the JPMorgan All Country Research Enhanced Equity ETF (JALL) on NYSE Arca. JALL expands the firm's research enhanced suite by offering a single, actively managed ETF for core global equity exposure across developed and emerging markets. The fund is seeded with $250 million at launch by FM, a leading commercial property insurer. As the largest issuer of active ETFs globally1, J.P. Morgan Asset Management continues to build a broad, differentiated active ETF range designed to help clients diversify portfolios and access institutional-quality active management. Morgan Asset Management. "As part of our continued commitment to expanding our active ETF platform, this launch seeks to give clients a simple way to diversify portfolios across the global equity market in a single wrapper." "As a long-term institutional investor, we see value in strategies that seek incremental alpha while maintaining the characteristics and diversification of a broad market portfolio. JALL brings this approach to global equities through an ETF structure," said Sanjay Chawla, Executive Vice President and Chief Investment Officer, FM. "Our experience with J.P. Morgan's research enhanced approach has given us confidence in the team's disciplined investment process, focus on fundamental stock selection and prudent risk management." According to J.P. As a portion of international equity ETF flows, active strategies increased to represent over 30% year-to-date 2026, underscoring investor interest in these products for global diversification. JALL targets the global large stock blend segment, one of the largest active equity ETF categories, delivering core exposure through a differentiated, actively managed research-backed process. title: Fixed income: A high-conviction opportunity - J.P. Morgan Private Bank

The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Fixed income is both a diversifier and one of our highest-conviction ideas. Bond yields today are the most attractive they've been in twenty years, and that means something simple for investors: you can now earn a genuine total return from income alone, not just downside protection. Per J.P. Morgan’s 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMA), global aggregate bond return forecasts have risen from a low of 2.1% in 2021 to 5.3% today, and global sovereign bonds offer their best return forecasts since the post-financial-crisis era. This is a structural shift, not a cyclical blip, and one investors can participate in today. The case is straightforward. Per the 2027 LTCMA’, the 10-year U.S. Treasury offers a 5.1% yield and a 10–15 year expected return of 5.5%; the 30-year offers a 5.4% yield and a 6.2% expected return. Investment grade (IG) credit yields 6.3% for a 6.1% expected return — the best in over twenty years — while high yield offers 8.5% for a 6.7% expected return, and emerging market debt offers 7.0% for a 6.5% expected return. These are the highest global bond return forecasts in two decades, and a decisive break from the unusually low returns of the post-financial-crisis era. The driver is structural: real yields have normalised, creating what the LTCMA calls a "compelling entry point." Higher growth and larger fiscal deficits imply higher real rates and larger term premia, pushing starting yields and embedded forward returns meaningfully higher. Context matters too. The LTCMA also raised our global equity forecast by 50bps to 7.5%, a constructive outlook in its own right. But the gap between equity and high-quality bond expected returns has narrowed sharply, and on a risk-adjusted basis the comparison now favours fixed income — sovereign bond Sharpe ratios have improved with higher starting yields and steeper curves, while equity Sharpe ratios are little changed. For investors used to thinking of bonds as a low-returning hedge, this is a regime change worth acting on. Starting yield has historically been one of the strongest predictors of forward bond returns. When yields have entered a period at today's levels, realised returns over the following several years have tended to cluster meaningfully higher than when starting yields were compressed — precisely the dynamic behind the LTCMA's two-decade-best forecasts. Past performance is never a guarantee, but the mechanics are simple. A higher coupon today compounds into a higher floor for total return tomorrow, and today's normalised real yields leave far less of that return dependent on price appreciation or duration risk. The hard work of waiting out the rate cycle has largely been done — the opportunity now is to earn the income. Fixed income continues to play a powerful role alongside equities. The LTCMA expects the correlation between global equities and U.S. aggregate bonds to be around 34% going forward, but it is explicit that "we still expect high-quality fixed income to have the lowest correlation to equities among liquid assets." Bonds remain a versatile tool: duration continues to be a strong hedge against demand-driven slowdowns, while inflation-linked and real assets can complement it when shocks come from the supply side. At the portfolio level, the math is compelling. The LTCMA's balanced global 60/40 stock-bond portfolio is projected to return 7.0%, up 60bp from last year's edition, with bonds contributing both income and ballast. This is a long-term, structural case for fixed income as a core allocation, not a tactical trade. Higher yields also make fixed income a more powerful planning tool — a meaningful, more predictable income stream can help investors fund specific long-term goals, such as retirement income, liability matching or legacy planning. Depending on their goals and preferences, investors can access this opportunity in many ways, from diversified bond funds and actively managed strategies to individual bond portfolios and ladders matched to future cash needs. Underpinning all of this is strong corporate fundamentals: issuers are often cash-rich and, per the LTCMA, "quite savvy in their debt management," supporting the case for high-quality credit. Economic nationalism is, per the LTCMA, "a modest growth risk but a greater risk to inflation." Elevated inflation volatility is expected to persist, particularly in higher-deficit nations such as the U.S., where continued deficits, debt brinkmanship and pressure on central bank independence could gradually weaken policy credibility and the "safe asset" premium. Supply chain, energy and security related themes are also current factors, which ideally calm. Credit markets are evolving too. Many governments face high debt, while corporations — often cash-rich and incentivized by shareholders to manage debt responsibly — now compare favourably on a relative risk basis. This quality theme has led the LTCMA to tighten its equilibrium credit spread assumptions, even as credit return projections generally keep pace with sovereign forecasts. On the upside, a genuine productivity renaissance driven by AI and a sustained investment super cycle could lift total factor productivity, limiting the rise in equilibrium real yields and supporting more stable, higher-quality returns across fixed income. Elevated yields, return forecasts at two-decade highs, lasting diversification benefits and strong corporate fundamentals add up to a compelling case. High-quality fixed income deserves a meaningful place in long-term, multi-asset, goals-based portfolios today. The opportunity is here, and investors can put it to work now, earning income levels not seen in a generation. Bond return forecasts are at two-decade highs, with structurally normalised real yields offering a compelling entry point. Investors can earn generation-high income levels now rather than waiting out further rate cycles. Key risks include economic nationalism and its pressure on inflation, persistent fiscal deficits weakening the "safe asset" premium and threats to central bank independence. Supply chain, energy and security-related themes are additional factors to monitor. The article doesn't address U.K. gilts specifically, but its broader thesis applies: higher starting sovereign yields globally translate into higher expected forward returns and a better income floor for long-term investors. While the article focuses on income rather than rate-cut scenarios, it notes duration remains a strong hedge against demand-driven slowdowns, implying price gains if rates fall amid weaker growth. High-quality fixed income is expected to retain the lowest correlation to equities among liquid assets, with a projected ~34% equity-bond correlation going forward. This supports bonds' role as ballast, helping the LTCMA's 60/40 portfolio forecast rise to 7.0%. Opportunities span U.S. Treasuries, investment grade and high-yield credit, and emerging market debt, each offering historically attractive yields and expected returns. The structural driver is normalised real yields and larger term premia from higher growth and fiscal deficits worldwide. title: Why Is JPMorgan Chase (JPM) Naming Bregje De Best As Its Next CFO? - Simply Wall St
content:
For readers looking to broaden their watchlist with related plays on the financial and technology backbone of markets, start with 53 AI infrastructure stocks. JPMorgan Chase operates as a large US bank and financial holding company across North America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia Pacific, Latin America, and the Caribbean, so a planned CFO transition affects how this global platform manages risk, capital, and regulatory relationships across multiple regions. Does the team leading JPMorgan Chase have what it takes? See our full breakdown of the management team's track record and compensation. The planned move from Jeremy Barnum to Bregje de Best reinforces JPMorgan Chase’s Narrative catalyst around converting heavy AI, payments and digital banking investment into durable earnings, while keeping the rising expense base under tighter stewardship. A long, multi year overlap between the two finance chiefs supports continuity around funding choices like the recent slate of long dated notes and the higher 2026 expense outlook of about US$107.5b. For investors, this change leans more toward reinforcing the growth and payments technology catalysts than altering the core risk that costs could run ahead of revenue. See how these catalysts shape JPMorgan Chase's path to a $376 fair value. The clearest waypoint to watch is how de Best and Barnum frame expense guidance and technology spend in the 2027 Investor Day and first quarter 2027 earnings materials when the handover completes, including any shift in targets for funding costs, net interest income and returns on those large AI and payments projects.
